messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo, a 55-year-old Navy Officer with a distinguished record, sat rigidly in the chair, his posture a stark contrast to the tremor in his hands. It had been eight months since he had returned from a trip to his home country, a trip intended to be a long-overdue family visit that had instead coincided with the eruption of a violent civil conflict. He was on a crowded street, heading towards a market to meet his cousin, when the first mortar struck. The world dissolved into a cacophony of shattering stone, screams, and the thick, acrid smell of explosives and dust. In the chaos, he, an unarmed man in civilian clothes, had scrambled for cover behind a collapsed fruit stall, his training screaming at him to act, to organize, to help. But all he could do was press himself into the dirt and wait for the carnage to end, a helpless witness to the suffering around him.

The memories of that day do not fade; they detonate. Often, a memory will come back to him not as a thought, but as a full-sensory assault. The sudden clang of a dropped tool on the deck of his ship can instantly transport him back to the market, the smell of cordite filling his nostrils and the phantom sensation of grit in his mouth. In these moments, it feels completely real, as if he is there again, and the reliving is always followed by a wave of profound, suffocating guilt. The images of those he couldn't help—a woman reaching out, a child crying—are seared into his mind. He sees their faces, and the belief that he should have protected them, that he failed in his most basic duty as a man and an officer, crashes over him. It is this conviction of his own failure that cements the memory, branding it not just as a tragedy he witnessed, but as a personal indictment.

This cycle of self-recrimination has become the engine of his distress. His belief that he is fundamentally a weak person, a coward who froze when it mattered, now actively summons the past. During a recent naval exercise, when he hesitated for a split second before issuing a command, the internal whisper started: *weakness*. That single thought was enough to open the floodgates. The feeling of inadequacy in the present instantly connected to his perceived failure in the past, and the market scene erupted in his mind’s eye, a vivid confirmation of the verdict he had already passed on himself. He has come to believe he will never forgive himself for not doing more, and this unforgiving stance acts as a constant invitation for the traumatic memories to return and provide their brutal evidence.

The constant loop between memory and self-blame has eroded the man he once was. He moves through his duties on the ship with a brittle efficiency, his mind a minefield. His partner has noted a growing distance, an emotional unavailability that frightens her. Sometimes, Mateo will try to explain what happened, but the words come out flat and disconnected. He can recall the sequence of events with a strange numbness, narrating the horror as if it happened to a stranger, a detached quality that feels more alienating than his silence. This emotionless recall is almost as disturbing as the flashbacks; it feels like another sign of his brokenness, another piece of evidence for the weakness he is certain has taken root inside him.

It was after he found himself drafting a letter of early retirement, convinced he was no longer fit to lead, that his partner insisted he seek help. Mateo came to therapy not with hope, but with a quiet sense of dread. He is terrified that talking about the event will only prove what he already believes to be true: that he is a weak man who failed, and that the uniform he wears is a costume he no longer deserves.
